stories.headline: Shop owners all over China started holding the same red banner: "Ban food delivery, shut down livestreams." State TV found they were paying a marketing firm 3,800 yuan a month to say it.
stories.what: Short videos showed owners of small physical shops holding a red banner reading "cancel delivery, shut down livestreams, bring back real shops". On 10 Nov CCTV traced the wave to Sichuan Shizhou Culture Media, a Yibin company registered in March 2026, running a brand called Sichuan Tongzhou Hui. Its operator, known online as Binlang Ge, sold shops account management, reportedly 3,800 yuan a month for 15 videos; the banner was the hook.
stories.twist: The protesters weren't protesting: a banquet restaurant had never offered delivery, another shop still did delivery, and one was a clothing shop. The operator admitted on camera the banner was a tested template, made deliberately low-quality, for 'violent account growth'. On 11 Nov Yibin's cyberspace office, police and market regulator formed a joint investigation team, ordered the company to stop and began investigating the people in charge; the account went private.
stories.why: A grassroots protest against the internet turned out to be an internet growth hack, and the 'restaurant' was a clothing shop.
stories.result: Verified (CCTV via The Paper, CNR, Guangming, China Economic Net, Jiemian, Sina Finance): joint investigation team formed 11 Nov; company ordered to stop. Fee reported by SMZDM. Penalties unknown yet.
stories.dates: Template videos autumn 2026 · CCTV exposé 10 Nov 2026 · joint investigation 11 Nov 2026 · still unfolding
stories.note: Entertainment 8 · Narrative 9 · Business 9 · Evidence 8 · Freshness 10. Footage: CCTV report video (shows banner videos, shops, operator's admission); original banner videos not found (account private). Opener: shopkeeper holding the red banner, hard cut to the clothes rails behind it. Never say the shops committed fraud; investigation targets the agency's people, no findings yet. No English coverage found.

stories.headline: He begged shoppers not to buy his scarves. Now he needs private security guards, the police have been called, and he opened an online shop.
stories.what: UPDATE of 2026-11-04-B-1. The Namdaemun Market scarf man (Hanyangsa, six scarves for 10,000 won) went viral telling customers not to buy. He reopened on 4 Nov; about 100 people blocked the alley, neighbours complained, police were called; he closed again on 5 Nov.
stories.twist: He hired three private security guards, stopped publishing his hours and opened an online shop; the Korea Herald reports early orders sold out. Jung-gu district plans to add the market to the government's crowd-management system.
stories.why: The anti-salesman became the most mobbed seller in Seoul.
stories.result: Reported: online sell-out (Korea Herald only); closures, police and guards (Financial News, Wikitree, Korea Times). Sales unknown.
stories.dates: Viral from 25 Oct 2026 · closures 31 Oct and 5 Nov · guards and online shop early-mid Nov · Korea Times follow-up 12 Nov
stories.note: Entertainment 7 · Narrative 7 · Business 8 · Evidence 6 · Freshness 9. Candidate, not a pick: online sell-out has a single source; no ending yet. Show only if the owner liked 2026-11-04-B-1.
